title: Where Detectors Fail: Probing Generative Space for Generalizable AI-Generated Image Detection
claim: Detectors trained on seen generators misclassify unseen fakes; steering the generator with detector feedback creates boundary samples that reshape the decision boundary.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, feature-space scatter plots flanking a central generator-detector loop
description: Three panels read left to right. Panels (a) and (c) are 2-D embedding scatter plots on gray backgrounds. Blue points are real images, orange are seen fakes, pink are unseen fakes, and green are boundary-induced fakes. Starred centroids are labeled, and a dashed navy line marks the decision boundary. In (a), a dotted red circle around the unseen fakes carries a red X and the word "Misclassify". The center panel (b) has a green dashed border. It shows an orange "Seen Generator" box on top and a blue "Detector" box below. Between them, arrows carry a fake image through two histograms, with a magnifier and a "judgment reward" feedback arrow. Dashed curves link the seen-fake cluster to a new scatter of green boundary-induced fakes. Panel (c) shows the shifted boundary, a green check, and the label "Correct".
caption: \wj{\name: Improving detector generalization via boundary-induced fake samples. (a) A detector trained on real images and samples from seen generators often fails to generalize to unseen generators, leading to misclassification of unseen fake images. (b) PROBE uses the detector as a critic to guide a seen generator toward challenging regions of the generative space. By steering generation based on detector feedback, PROBE produces boundary-induced fake samples that expose failure modes of the detector while remaining visually realistic. (c) Fine-tuning the detector on these boundary-induced fake samples reshapes the decision boundary, improving robustness and enabling correct classification of previously unseen fake images. }
abstract: Detecting AI-generated images (AIGI) remains challenging because detectors often fail to generalize to unseen generators. Although existing methods are trained on large datasets, their performance still degrades when generation settings change, indicating that data scale alone is insufficient and that limited coverage of generative variations during training is a key factor. Studies on generative model editing show that small changes in internal representations can produce diverse and meaningful image variations, many of which are not explored under standard sampling. Leveraging this insight, we propose PROBE (Probing Robustness via Boundary Exploration), a framework that improves detector generalization by actively exploring challenging regions of the generative process. Instead of treating the generator as a fixed data source, PROBE uses the detector as a critic to steer the generator through manifold-level modifications, producing realistic samples that are difficult to classify. These samples expose failure cases that are uncommon under standard data sampling strategies and are used to refine the detector. Experimental results across multiple benchmarks indicate that PROBE enhances generalization to unseen generators, resulting in more generalizable AIGI detection performance. Code and models are available at https://github.com/Amamiya-C/PROBE-AIGI-Detection
